location.name: The second Lagrange point, 1.5 million km from Earth

creator.name: NASA, ESA and CSA; Northrop Grumman; the Space Telescope Science Institute

object.description: A mirror six and a half metres across, eighteen gold-plated beryllium hexagons, folded to fit inside a rocket and opened in space over two weeks, standing on a sunshield the size of a tennis court that keeps it colder than minus 220 degrees so it can see in infrared: the heat-light of the first galaxies, stretched by the expansion of the universe past the reach of any eye or of Hubble. It was twenty-five years in the making and sits a million and a half kilometres away, where no one can go to fix it; 344 things had to deploy in order and every one did. Six months after launch it sent back the deepest picture of the universe ever taken, which hangs on the next row.
facts: The mirror's gold is 48 grams in all, a layer a few hundred atoms thick; gold reflects infrared best.
It sees in infrared because light from the first galaxies has been stretched more than tenfold on its way to us.
Launched on an Ariane 5 from French Guiana so precisely that the fuel saved doubled its expected life, to twenty years.
It has found galaxies from 300 million years after the big bang, earlier and brighter than the models predicted.
